idiom_name: ActiveJob class method (perform_later) with a configured queue adapter
implementation_notes: Rails supplies the one-way gateway: the domain method is a job class's class method - GuestsCleanupJob.perform_later(guest), with .set(wait:/wait_until:) for scheduling and perform_all_later for batches - and the queue adapter (Solid Queue by default in Rails 8, or Sidekiq/Resque/...) is chosen in configuration, so the caller never sees the broker. What replaces the classic gateway class is one job class per message plus the adapter; you write the interface, the framework writes the plumbing. A request-reply gateway (a method that returns a value) is not covered: that correlation has to be built over AMQP with Bunny (basic_publish with reply_to/correlation_id plus a reply consumer), which is the manual route.
code_sketch:
class StockCheck < ApplicationJob               # the gateway method
  queue_as :inventory

  def perform(sku)
    Inventory::Client.check(sku)                # messaging hidden from callers
  end
end

StockCheck.perform_later("SKU-42")              # caller: method call, no broker types
StockCheck.set(wait: 5.minutes).perform_later("SKU-42")
pitfalls: perform_later returns false instead of raising when Active Job traps an enqueue error, so a gateway that ignores the return value silently drops messages.

Delivery semantics belong to the adapter: the development async adapter keeps jobs in RAM and loses the whole backlog on restart, while production defaults to a database-backed queue - the same call has different guarantees per environment.

Enqueue timing relative to a database transaction is backend-dependent (enqueue_after_transaction_commit exists precisely because of that), so callers must not assume the message is published when their transaction commits.
There is no reply: perform_later resolves to a job id at best, so a caller expecting a value must not be modelled on ActiveJob.
